title: The Ferryman

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha becomes Vasudeva's assistant. Vasudeva, a simple and attentive listener, teaches him to listen to the river, which shows that there is no such thing as time—the river is everywhere at once. Years pass peacefully. Gotama's monks pass by, carrying news that the Buddha is dying, and Kamala travels with her son to see him; she is bitten by a snake, recognizes Siddhartha at the ferry, and dies in his arms. Siddhartha keeps their son.

vocabulary.context: They travelled to seek money and business, and for weddings, and on pilgrimages, and the river was obstructing their path, and the ferryman’s job was to get them quickly across that obstacle.

vocabulary.definition: Ripe or mature before the proper or natural time
vocabulary.context: They had been, so it seemed to him, proud and precocious words; with a smile, he remembered them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To carry or transport over a river, strait, or other narrow water, in a boat
vocabulary.context: Behold, once before you have ferried me across this water in your boat for the immaterial reward of a good deed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: One who uses, or is skilled in the use of, an oar
vocabulary.context: The rich and elegant Siddhartha is becoming an oarsman’s servant, the learned Brahmin Siddhartha becomes a ferryman: this has also been told to you by the river.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: In a wonderful or surprising manner or degree
vocabulary.context: He looked up and first saw the boy’s face, which wondrously reminded him of something, like a warning to remember something he had forgotten.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: The town, city, or country, where a person is born
vocabulary.context: Listening carefully, he let everything enter his mind, birthplace and childhood, all that learning, all that searching, all joy, all distress.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: And with that singsong, the boy became calm, was only now and then uttering a sob and fell asleep.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To fall together suddenly, as the sides of a hollow vessel
vocabulary.context: Hurriedly, they now both ran along the path, in order to reach people, and got near to the ferry, there Kamala collapsed, and was not able to go any further.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: A lot it has told me, deeply it has filled me with the healing thought, with the thought of oneness.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To bite and grind with the teeth
vocabulary.context: She, Kamala herself, had also become tired, and while the boy was chewing a banana, she crouched down on the ground, closed her eyes a bit, and rested.

context.history: The image of the river echoes ancient ideas, such as Heraclitus's saying that one cannot step into the same river twice.

significance: The listening river replaces human teachers; Kamala's peaceful death and the son's arrival begin a new test.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “The Ferryman,” how does Hesse show learning from the river? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the symbolism you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Ferryman develops the idea of learning from the river. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of symbolism and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses symbolism in The Ferryman to complicate the reader's understanding of learning from the river. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Ferryman within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of learning from the river responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Ferryman as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of learning from the river. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

satQuestions.passage: “Now I recognise you,” he finally said. “At one time, you’ve slept in my hut, this was a long time ago, possibly more than twenty years ago, and you’ve been ferried across the river by me, and we parted like good friends. Haven’t you been a Samana? I can’t think of your name any more.”

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: What does the river teach that no person could? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include obstructing, precocious, ferried, oarsman, wondrously. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “They travelled to seek money and business, and for weddings, and on pilgrimages, and the river was obstructing their path, and the ferryman’s job was to get them quickly across that obstacle.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To block up.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. The image of the river echoes ancient ideas, such as Heraclitus's saying that one cannot step into the same river twice. Now, why does this chapter matter? The listening river replaces human teachers; Kamala's peaceful death and the son's arrival begin a new test. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Symbolism, Characterization, Theme.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot symbolism, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
segments.passage: “Now I recognise you,” he finally said. “At one time, you’ve slept in my hut, this was a long time ago, possibly more than twenty years ago, and you’ve been ferried across the river by me, and we parted like good friends. Haven’t you been a Samana? I can’t think of your name any more.”
